fields.sample_size: 101 developing countries (WatSan4Dev subset of 25 variables; five thematic pillars HDP, CEC, AP, ODA, WR)
fields.effect_measure: Bayesian network probabilistic modelling: general water-supply and sanitation models plus thematic models; validated by classification error rate, log/quadratic loss and spherical payoff; scenario analysis by recomputed probabilities (Table 10)
fields.effect_estimate: Classification error rates under 12% (water supply) and under 10% (sanitation); thematic models 5-20%. Scenario results (probability changes): raising the human-development-and-poverty composite (HDP) to HIGH raises the probability of high WS by 35.9 and of high sanitation by 34.5 points; GDP per capita HIGH +53, urban population +43, slums LOW +31.9, child mortality LOW +33.7 on HDP; government effectiveness (WGI GE, which also represents control of corruption) HIGH +24.8 on HDP; voice and accountability HIGH +23.8 on country environmental concern. The authors read advanced governance (government effectiveness, control of corruption, rule of law, regulatory quality) as favourable to WSS sustainability, but the links are probabilistic associations between composite indicators, not causal effects; water-resource variables are used descriptively.
fields.study_design: cross-national ecological modelling study (101 developing countries; Bayesian networks)
fields.section: Full text (Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci. 17:3397-3419): 2 Data; 3 Methodology; 4 Modelling (4.1 general models, 4.2 thematic pillars, 4.3 country profiles); 5 Discussions; 6 Conclusions; Table 10
fields.exact_location: 2.1 variables p3399-3400 (WGI defined as basic/advanced governance); 4.1 validation p3404; Table 10 scenarios p3412; Conclusions p3412-3413

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a Bayesian network modelling study of 101 developing countries (25 WatSan4Dev variables), read in full text 2026-10-04. Models show associations among human development, governance, urbanisation and water/sanitation access (classification error under 10-12%); governance effectiveness is positively associated with the human-development composite. Ecological, probabilistic, non-causal.
